Family Man Beat To Death By Migrant Teenagers In Dublin.

On Sunday 17 May 2026, at around 4:15pm on Mill Road in Blanchardstown, 37-year-old Alex Coughlan was attacked by two 16-year-old boys without warning.

The defenceless Irishman was forced to his knees, pleading for mercy as one teenager repeatedly punched and kicked him in the head. 

The second boy filmed the assault on his mobile phone. Alex screamed for help and begged them to stop. He had already handed over his wallet and bank cards, but hesitated when they demanded his gold ring, a gift from his father.

That moment of hesitation cost him his life.

The beating continued. Alex was left unconscious on the ground. He died three days later on 20 May in Connolly Hospital from catastrophic head injuries. His family made the selfless decision to donate his organs.

Two 16-year-old boys were arrested and charged with assault causing serious harm and robbery. The main attacker is a second-generation migrant born and raised in Ireland. The other, who filmed the attack, is a migrant with dual nationality. Both were described by locals as having non-native features. 

Gardai later recovered the stolen ring from one of the boys homes, and Alex’s father identified it in court.

The teenagers appeared in Dublin Children’s Court on 27 May. 

A judge imposed strict reporting restrictions, warning against naming them or sharing the video of the attack circulating online due to their age. 
Bail was refused, and both teenagers remain remanded in custody.

On Saturday 30 May, what would have been Alex’s 38th birthday, hundreds gathered in Ballyfermot to farewell him. He was remembered as the glue of his family, a kind, gentle, and selfless man who brought laughter and joy to everyone around him.

A dedicated Bupa worker and passionate rugby fan, Alex is survived by his mother Brigid, father John, sister Zara, and brothers Philip and Jack. Mourners sang Happy Birthday and Ireland’s Call. Tributes described him as a truly beautiful soul and caring human being. A private cremation followed at Glasnevin Cemetery.

While Alex’s funeral took place, the Irish mainstream media gave far more coverage and focused far more outrage on the death of Congolese national Yves Sakila, 35. Sakila, who had dozens of previous convictions and multiple prison terms for repeated shoplifting, died on 15 May after being restrained by security staff during another shoplifting attempt. His death was quickly framed by activists as Ireland’s George Floyd moment, sparking protests, political speeches, and claims of racism.

Alex’s killing, a local Irish family man robbed and beaten to death in broad daylight while pleading for mercy received far less attention. Coverage focused on the attackers age and anonymity, with zero discussion of backgrounds or nationalities. 

There were no mass candlelit vigils when Alex died, no major protests demanding justice, no political statements, and no national campaigns declaring that his life mattered.

No Netflix documentaries will ever examine Alex's final moments.

Certain tragedies fit a preferred political narrative and ignite weeks of outrage. Others, like the brutal murder of a gentle Irish family man, are treated as less newsworthy. This selective response from the Irish media and political class is an insult to Alex and every family who has lost someone in similar circumstances.

Alex Coughlan’s life mattered. He deserved better, and the people of Ireland deserve the truth.

RIP Alex Coughlan.

Lebanon’s Flag Carrier Is Flying Through a War — and Into a Conflict of Interest

Middle East Airlines has spent months selling itself as the stubborn lifeline of a collapsing country: still flying into Beirut while missiles fall, still propping up a dead currency with ticket sales and remittances. Now we find out the “heroism” may include dodging airstrikes and punishing pilots who say that’s insane.

According to pilot unions, MEA crews have been asked to operate routes threading through or near active strike zones while Israeli bombs land close enough to the Beirut airport to rattle windows and nerves. 

Pilots who file safety reports about mistakes or near-misses — the kind of reporting every modern safety system depends on — allegedly find themselves “sent for training,” which just happens to strip them of the per‑flight pay that makes up most of their income in a collapsed economy. 

When your base salary has been shredded by devaluation, “training” starts to look a lot like economic punishment.

Lebanon’s aviation regulator has now launched a safety audit of MEA, but the setup is almost a caricature: the state that’s supposed to police the airline is broke, its staff’s pay has been decimated, and MEA has been stepping in to “support” the very workers tasked with overseeing it. 

The airline admits it’s been topping up the wages of civil aviation employees — including safety staff — in the name of keeping the system running. In any other jurisdiction, that’s called a conflict of interest. In Lebanon, it’s called survival.

Pilot groups are so uneasy they’ve gone over Beirut’s head to the SkyTeam alliance, nudging big partners like Air France and Delta with a simple question: do you really know how your Lebanese codeshare is managing risk while rockets and drones redraw the map? 

Everyone, of course, responds with the usual corporate liturgy: safety is our top priority, we audit regularly, we are monitoring the situation. 

Meanwhile, the same crews who fly those metal tubes are saying, on the record, that speaking up can cost them money and that flying “heroic” routes in an active war zone is being normalized.

MEA insists its record is clean, that every flight is based on proper risk assessment coordinated with the regulator, that all this is an overblown union panic. Maybe. 

But when the airline pays the people who oversee it, operates out of an airport that’s had strikes land nearby, and depends on desperate, underpaid pilots to keep the country connected, you don’t need a crash to see the systemic risk. 

You just need to look at who is being asked to take the danger — and who keeps cashing in on calling it resilience.

Found in tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide—and in the Atlantic, even extending into north temperate waters—this unique cephalopod has a mantle that grows up to 10 centimeters (about four inches) long. Inside, glass squids have a large cavity filled with ammonium, a substance lighter than seawater. This clever adaptation increases buoyancy, reducing the need for constant swimming. Instead, they glide slowly through the open ocean using their fins, ever watchful for threats—or their next meal.
